# Biological problem

The main biological question that drives the RNA bulk sequencing in this
study, is understanding the translocation kinetics of NF-κB by measuring
the transcriptional consequences associated with the amount of time the
p65 subunit remains in the nucleus in both MED12-KO and MED24-KO HeLa
cells. However this methodological step is not the main objective of
this study, but a validation pipeline of a novel technological approach
proposed: Optical Pooled Screening.

# Objective

To perform a comparative temporal transcriptomic profiling between 1 hour  vs. 4 hour timepoints of MED12-KO and MED24-KO HeLa cells under IL-1β and TNF-α stimulation, utilizing a multi-package diferential gene intersection approach to isolate high-confidence deregulated pathways.

# Experimental design

## Wet-lab protocol

The methodology of Optical Pooled Screens in Human Cells presented by
Feldman D. and collaborators explores a novel platform of massive
optical screening that allows linking engineered genetic perturbations
to cellular phenotypes in millions of fixed cells. The methodology is
based on the delivery of CRISPR libraries using lentiviral vectors and
in situ sequencing by synthesis using padlock probes followed by rolling
circle amplification. This study focused on the NF-κB signaling pathway,
which was induced by the administration of IL-1β and TNF-α, and
evaluated nuclear translocation of p65, a NF-κB subunit in more than 3
million cells.

A LentiGuide-Puro vector was engineered to carry a sgRNA and a Pol
II-transcribed antibiotic resistance gene containing a 12-nt barcode
flanked by constant sequences on its 3’ UTR region, the authors named
this modified version LentiGuide-BC. A low multiplicity infection
transduction (MOI \< 0.01) was performed to ensure an individual
integration per cell. The barcodes expressed as mRNA were detected using
targeted in situ sequencing, the mRNA sequences were converted into cDNA
and hybridized with padlock probes, ligated by enzymatic ligation and
further amplified by rolling circle amplification. These products of
amplification underwent a 12-cycle sequencing by synthesis under low
magnification microscopy (10x), enabling high-throughput analysis.
Sequences obtained from the imaging process were then compared to a
predesigned barcode dictionary of 83,314 barcodes, the 12-nt barcode
were synthetized using criteria that balanced GC content, minimized
homopolymer repeats, and maintained a minimum edit distance between each
of them.

To validate the precision of the system, a CRISPR system was implemented
on cell lines containing an inactive hemagglutinin (HA) gene frameshift
reporter. In this validation workflow the CRISPR-Cas system was designed
to target the inactive sequence of the HA gene and correct the
frameshift of the protein, thereby producing functional HA, which was
later detected using conjugated antibodies. When the in situ sequencing
was performed, 90.6% correspondence between the reporter activating RNA
guide and its expected barcode, demonstrating a high fidelity and
allowing it to be used in large-scale genomic libraries

For results validation and eliminating recombination artifacts a screen
beyond static points was performed, using a CROP-seq vector, which
expresses a Pol II-transcribed copy of the sgRNA that can be directly
read by in situ sequencing without an auxiliary barcode. Cas9 expression
was induced by a 14 day doxycycline treatment and cells were loaded with
Hoechst 33342 as a live nuclear stain. Cells were then stimulated with
IL-1B or TNF-A, and imaged at 23 minute intervals over 6 hours,
capturing 361,587 cells. This temporal approach revealed MED12 and MED24
as negative regulators, both prolonged p65 nuclear retention at time
points \>2 h.

To confirm MED12 and MED24 as bona fide hits, a high-coverage pooled
validation screen targeting 61 candidate genes at 10 sgRNAs per gene was
performed, confirming both genes with strong intra-gene sgRNA
concordance across cells.

Clonal homozygous knockout lines were then generated using synthetic
crRNA/tracrRNA duplexes to target MED12 and MED24 in the
HeLa-TetR-Cas9/p65-mNeonGreen cell lines. Both homozygosity knockout and
the expected p65 nuclear retention were validated by sequencing and
live-cell microscopy For bulk RNA sequencing, clones were stimulated
with TNF-α or IL-1β for 0, 1, or 4 hours and sequenced on a NextSeq 500
Illumina sequencer using a paired-end approach in 36 cycles.
Differential expression analysis using edgeR identified upregulation of
chemokine genes and and induction of pro-IL-1β by TNF-α exclusively in
MED12/MED24-deficient cells, implicating Mediator complex subunits as
suppressors of the NF-κB transcriptional response.

## Miami compliant

MINSEQE (Minimum Information About a Next-generation Sequencing
Experiment) guidelines are completely met. The documentation and data
can be found on the GEO database on with the registry ID "GSE132704".

# Data Processing and Analysis

## Data exploration

### Loading data

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(omicsdata)
library(limma)
library(EDASeq)
library(edgeR)
library(dplyr)
library(plyr)
library(corrplot)
library(ggfortify)


#data in summarized experiment 
#data = readRDS(("/opt/omicsdata/datasets/SRP201365.rds"))
#saveRDS(data, "DataSet.rds")

#retrieve from directory 
data <- readRDS("DataSet.rds")



RawExprMtx = assay(data)
```

### Sample's Info parsing

"sra.sample_attributes" contains experimental data in the
format:"key\|value;;key\|value".\
We extract the values into a clean data frame.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Extract RAW sample experimental data 
RawColumn = colData(data)$sra.sample_attributes

# Splitting "key|value;;key|value" formatting 
parse_attrs = function(x) {
  pairs  = strsplit(x, "\\|")[[1]]          
  values = sapply(strsplit(pairs, ";;"), `[`, 2)  
  values
}

# Applied to all samples, stored in dataframe 
ExperimentalInfo = as.data.frame(t(sapply(RawColumn, parse_attrs)),
                                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Name assignment, matching sample names
colnames(ExperimentalInfo) = c("cell_line", "clone", "genotype","source_name", 
                                "stimulation", "timepoint")

rownames(ExperimentalInfo) = colnames(RawExprMtx)
```

### Diagnostic plots

Before executing downstream Differential Expression and Over
Representation Analysis, robust quality control (QC) is performed to
assess global data distribution, identify potential batch effects, and
detect sample outliers.\
By evaluating the raw and log-transformed count matrices through visual
methods, such as distribution boxplots, Relative Log Expression (RLE)
profiles, we can comprehensively diagnose systematic variances and
evaluate the homogeneity of the experimental replicates across the
monitored timepoints (1h vs 4h).

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=12}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggfortify)


colores <- c("steelblue3", "indianred3", "seagreen4", 
             "tan1", "mediumpurple3", "yellowgreen")

ExperimentalInfo$Groups <- paste0(ExperimentalInfo$genotype, ExperimentalInfo$timepoint)

ExperGroups <- sort(unique(ExperimentalInfo$Groups))
colorMap <- setNames(colores, ExperGroups)
mapa_colores <- colorMap[ExperimentalInfo$Groups]
col = mapa_colores


par(mfrow = c(3,1), mar = c(5,4,2,1))

#Boxplot of log transformed counts
#objective: to evaluate and compare the overall distribution of gene expression 
#level across all samples. To detect sequencing depth discrepancies
boxplot(log1p(RawExprMtx), col = col, xlab = "Sample", ylab = "log1p expression",
        ylim = c(0, 20), las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7, 
        main = "Boxplot of log1p transformed expression")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap), col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)


#MA plot
#objective: to detect bias between expression intensity and log-fold change
limma::plotMA(log1p(RawExprMtx), main = "MA plot of log1p transformed expression", 
              xlab = "A", ylab = "M") 
legend("topright", legend = c("1h","4h"), col = 1:2, pch = 20, cex = 0.7, 
       ncol = 2, bty = "n") 

par(mfrow = c(3,1))
    
#pairwise mean difference (MD) plot
#to perform targeted comparisons between selected pairs of samples
MDPlot(RawExprMtx, c(1, 72),  main = "Mean-difference plot Sample 1 and 72")     
MDPlot(RawExprMtx, c(5, 20),  main = "Mean-difference plot Sample 5 and 20")   
MDPlot(RawExprMtx, c(37, 6),  main = "Mean-difference plot Sample 37 and 6")
```

Summary of QC Anomalies

Boxplot Analysis:\
The raw library distributions show a consistent median $log_{1p}$
expression level across the majority of the samples. However, three
obvious critical outliers exhibit severe distribution collapse:
SRR9297211, SRR9297243, and SRR9297255. These three anomalous samples
were excluded from the following steps of the pipeline to prevent
statistical bias.

MA Plot Analysis: At expression regimes $A > 6$, the data shows symmetry
tightly centered around the baseline ($M = 0$), highliting a stable
global transcriptome across samples. Conversely, at low expression
levels ($A < 5$), diagonal stripes emerge. This striping is a an
artifact of log-transformations applied to small discrete integer
counts, which are heavily dominated by Poisson noise. These later
features lack sufficient statistical power for robust differential
modeling, an expression filter (via edgeR's filterByExpr) was applied to
delete this before further testing.

Mean-Difference (MD) Plots Analysis To evaluate pairwise technical
variations and the presence of systematic scaling biases between
individual libraries, Mean-Difference (MD) plots were generated across
three representative sample pairs:\
- Sample 1 and 72 (Top panel):\
A severe downward trend is visible, with the lowess regression line
dropping sharply below the horizontal baseline ($M = 0$) as the mean
expression intensity increases. This strong negative skew indicates a
severe composition bias or pronounced batch effects between these
libraries.\
- Sample 5 and 20 (Middle panel):\
A mild downward curvature is observed in the high-expression regime
($A > 10$), indicating that although this pair exhibits better alignment
than the top panel, minor residual bias persists. This confirms that
simple library size scaling (such as CPM) is insufficient to eliminate
all non-biological variations, highlighting the need for multi-factor
normalization.

\- Sample 37 and 6 (Bottom panel):\
The ow trend line remains perfectly flat and aligned with the dashed
reference line ($M = 0$) across the entire dynamic range of gene
expression, presenting a diagnostic result showing very low technical
and compositional differences between these two libraries.

To identify the dominant drivers of global transcriptional variance and
assess potential technical batch effects, exploratory Principal
Component Analysis (PCA) was performed across the dataset.

Variance Distribution: Principal Component 1 (PC1) accounts for the vast
majority of total transcriptomic variance ($21.47\%$), whereas PC2
($3.24\%$) and PC3 ($2.28\%$) only capture ($3.24\%$) and ($2.28\%$)
respectively, but counter intuitively are the two PC that better split
the groups in biological meaningful manner.

Treatment Confounding Factor (First Figure): Visual overlay of treatment
conditions (IL-1, TNF-$\alpha$, and untreated) lack of spatial
separation demonstrates that exogenous cytokine treatments do not
introduce significant global batch effects.

Genotype Biological Driver (Second Figure): In contrast to the treatment
profiles, clear and distinct sample clustering is visible along the PC2
and PC3 coordinates. The wild-type (WT), MED12-KO, and MED24-KO groups
split into obvious isolated populations. These diagnostics confirm that
transcriptional variance is reliably driven by the primary biological
variable of interest: the cell Genotype.

### Exploratory PCA

```{r ,fig.width=11, fig.height=8}

EDASeq::plotPCA(RawExprMtx, k=3, labels=FALSE, col=col, pch=20) 
legend("right", legend = names(colorMap), col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n",cex = .7)
```

To have a first glance at global expression dynamics and determine the
sources of variance, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed on

labels.Principal Component 2 and 3 clearly separate wt samples from the
MED12 KO and MED24 KO groups, within the wt group, 1h (purple) and 4h

```{r ,fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
#PCA screen plot
pca = prcomp(t(log1p(RawExprMtx)))
screeplot(pca, type = c("lines"))
```
The scree plot displays a sharp, classic "elbow" transition at PC2,
confirming that PC1 captures the dominant fraction of global dataset
variance, however, PC2 and PC3 are better depicting de variability
between the biological and temporal groups.


```{r ,fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
EDASeq::plotPCA(RawExprMtx, k=2, labels=FALSE, pch=20, col = col, main = "Outlier Detection")
legend("right", legend = names(colorMap), col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n",cex = .7)

```

A visual assessment of sample distribution via PCA was performed, and sample-level filtering was done in the following code to samples with datapoints deviating by more than three standard deviations from the PC1 or PC2.



```{r ,fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
# Coordinate extraction 
pca_scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x)

# function to detect outliers (3 standard deviations)
detect_outliers <- function(column) {
  abs(column - mean(column)) > (3 * sd(column))
}

outliers_PC1 <- rownames(pca_scores)[detect_outliers(pca_scores$PC1)]
outliers_PC2 <- rownames(pca_scores)[detect_outliers(pca_scores$PC2)]

# Inspection 
outliers_names <- unique(c(outliers_PC1, outliers_PC2))
outliers = match(outliers_names, colnames(RawExprMtx))
```


The diagnostic plots validate that further analysis should only proceed
on the raw matrices directly. These exploratory analysis establishes two
evident exigencies: first, the exclusion of sample outliers, and the
application of a robust normalization framework to adress artifacts and
composition biases seen in the MD plots.

### GC content gene length

In high-throughput RNA-sequencing data workflows, two primary sources of
within-sample, gene-specific technical bias variation are gene length
and guanine-cytosine (GC) content. To isolate true biological variation
from these confounding technical artifacts, downstream normalization
strategies must be employed. These algorithms require the physical
properties of each genetic feature as input covariates which are
retrieved in the following code block, executing the database queries
required to isolate stable Ensembl identifiers and fetch the
corresponding length and nucleotide composition from the human reference
genome to adress this.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

#substring ENSMBL IDs 
ensid = substr(as.character(rowRanges(data)$gene_id), 1, 15) #remove version of the gene
rowData(data)$ensid = ensid

#for each gene compute GC content and Length retrieval using human genome database
gc = getGeneLengthAndGCContent(id = ensid, org = "hg38", mode = "org.db")

```

### Matrices filtering

Unannotated genetic features, duplicated entries, and genes with missing
structural metadata (such as missing GC-content or length values) lack
the necessary information for further normalization and biological
interpretation.

Prior to normalization "filterByExpr" from the edgeR package, algorithm
from the edgeR package was applied to establish a minimum threshold of
reads across replicates, lowcount genes that would only artificially
increase variance.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
gc   = gc[!is.na(gc[, 2]), ] #remove genes without information
data = data[rowData(data)$ensid %in% rownames(gc), ] #keep on database only genes with information
#data and gc have the same genes now

#remove duplicates
dup       = duplicated(rownames(gc)) #list of true and false
gc        = gc[!dup, ] #remove duplicates from gc
data      = data[!dup, ] #remove duplicates from data

raw_count =  assay(data) #raw count matrix filtered

rownames(raw_count) = rownames(gc) #same names of genes (in rows)

# Setting groups and filtering by "filterByExpr"
keep = filterByExpr(raw_count, group = ExperimentalInfo$Groups)  
expr_filtered_w_outliers = raw_count[keep, ] #extract genes where keep=TRUE
expr_filtered <- expr_filtered_w_outliers[, -outliers]

# Keep data and gc in sync with the filtered count matrix
ExprSel = data[rowData(data)$ensid %in% rownames(expr_filtered), ]
ExprSel <- ExprSel[, !(colnames(ExprSel) %in% outliers_names)]
gc_sel   = gc[rownames(expr_filtered), ]

#Delete outliers from experimental info 
ExperimentalInfo <- ExperimentalInfo[!(rownames(ExperimentalInfo) %in% outliers_names), ]
#to compare data before and after filtering

PlotDF = rbind(
  data.frame(sums = rowSums(raw_count),     status = "Before"),
  data.frame(sums = rowSums(expr_filtered), status = "After")
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Define a shared Y-axis
shared_ylim <- c(0, 0.75)

# Plot BEFORE filtering
log_cpm_before <- log2(edgeR::cpm(raw_count) + 1)
mean_log_cpm_before <- rowMeans(log_cpm_before)

plot(density(mean_log_cpm_before), 
     main = "Before Filtering\n(29,775 genes)", 
     xlab = "Mean Log2 CPM", 
     ylab = "Density", 
     col = "tan1", lwd = 2,
     ylim = shared_ylim) 
abline(v = 0, col = "gray", lty = 2)

# Plot AFTER filtering
log_cpm_after <- log2(edgeR::cpm(expr_filtered) + 1)
mean_log_cpm_after <- rowMeans(log_cpm_after)

plot(density(mean_log_cpm_after), 
     main = "After Filtering\n(15,828 genes)", 
     xlab = "Mean Log2 CPM", 
     ylab = "Density", 
     col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2,
     ylim = shared_ylim) 
abline(v = 0, col = "gray", lty = 2)

```

The figure shows the density distribution of gene expression levels
before and after low-expression filtering. The X-axis represent a
standardized measure of gene expression leves in a $\log_2$ scale, the
Y-axis shows the proportion of genes that share a specific expression
value.

Before filtering, the density plot shows a massive peak around 0,
indicating that a large number of the 29.775 genes have very low or zero
expression level, which represent the background noise. After filtering,
the dataset was reduced to 15828 genes, resulting in a more balanced
distribution, suitable for differential expression analysis.

The density plots confirm that the filtering pipeline successfully
separated uninformative technical background noise from true biological
signal.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, boxplot-norm, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}
#boxplot for outliers removal
# objective: to verify the successful removal of low-quality sample outliers by 
#comparing total sequencing depth across the dataset

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(log2(raw_count + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(count+1)",
        main = "Raw counts", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

boxplot(log2(expr_filtered + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(count+1)",
        main = "Raw counts without outliers ", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The figure above shows the impact on the dataset of removing three
outliers. The X-axis represent biological samples, while the Y-axis
represent the log-transformed gene expression level, calculated as
$\log_2(Count + 1)$.

During the PCA exploratory analysis, outliers were statistically
detected and defined as samples whose coordinates exceeded three
standard deviations from the mean along either the first or second
principal component. This mathematical threshold flagged three samples
as low-quality sequencing libraries, which were subsequently excluded
from downstream analysis.

The PCA-filtering successfully removed the extreme outliers, from the
plot in the right panel is visible that two samples continue to exhibit
distinct structural profiles in the cleaned dataset, with higher
variance and a larger proportion of low-expressed genes. Despite these
reasons, these 2 samples were retained in the dataset because their
median expression level remains aligned and they did not exceed the
mathematical threshold of 3 standard deviation.

## Normalization

Since sequencing datasets are heavily influenced by the technical
process of sequencing itself, the primary aim of normalization is to
remove systematic technical variation between samples, so it will be
possible to compare their true biological differences.

Technical biases in RNA-Seq architectures operate across two distinct dimensions: intra-sample (within-lane) and inter-sample (between-lane) variables, each requiring targeted algorithmic correction to preserve data integrity.

Within-lane artifacts distort the relative expression profiles of genomic features within a single discrete library. These variations are predominantly driven by the physical architecture of the transcripts, specifically transcript length and nucleotide composition. During cDNA fragmentation, longer transcripts naturally yield a higher absolute mass of fragments, artificially inflating their raw read counts relative to shorter transcripts of identical cellular abundance. Concurrently, local Guanine-Cytosine (GC) content skews data distribution due to thermal stability differentials during polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification and cluster generation, leading to the systematic underrepresentation of genomic regions with extreme GC ratios.

Inter-Sample distortions occur across
different samples, compromising the comparability of
the dataset. They are primarily driven by variations in sequencing depth
(total library size differences between lanes) and compositional bias
(highly expressed master transcripts depleting the sequencing resources
available for low-abundance genes).

Conversely, between-lane distortions compromise comparability across distinct sequencing tracks and independent biological samples. These variations are primarily driven by discrepancies in absolute sequencing depth, resulting from unequal sample pooling or variable cluster densities on the flow cell.  
Furthermore, inter-sample analysis is highly susceptible to RNA compositional bias, a phenomenon where a restricted cohort of highly expressed transcripts monopolizes a disproportionate share of the total sequencing throughput. This over representation mathematically depletes the remaining read budget available for low-abundance transcripts, inducing false observations of global downregulation in unnormalized datasets. 

To establish an optimal scaling and artifact-correction architecture capable of standardizing these distribution variances across all 76 independent libraries, two parallel exploratory normalization tracks were executed and evaluated.

To determine an optimal scaling and artifact-correction architecture
able to standardize the variance for our dataset across all 76 independent libraries, two parallel exploratory normalization tracks were executed and evaluated.

### Initialization of data structure SeqExpressionSet

To prepare the data for within-lane normalization and diagnostic
tracking, EDASeq package was used to create a SeqExpressionSet object,
which integrates the filtered raw count matrix with both sample-level
metadata (phenoData) and gene-specific biophysical covariates
(featureData), satisfying a mandatory requirement for normalization
algorithm.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(EDASeq)

set = newSeqExpressionSet(
          expr_filtered, #filtered counts
          phenoData = AnnotatedDataFrame( #metadata, information on samples
                          data.frame(
                          conditions = factor(1:ncol(expr_filtered)),
                          row.names = colnames(expr_filtered))),
          featureData = AnnotatedDataFrame( #info on gene length and gc content
                          data.frame(
                            gc = gc_sel[, 2], 
                            l = gc_sel[, 1])))
```

### Between lane Normalization

We compute four distinct between-lane scaling methods via the edgeR
ecosystem to evaluate global variance adjustments. Ultimately, the
Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) approach will be prioritized as our
definitive mathematical baseline for downstream differential expression
testing due to its superior capacity to handle compositional bias.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#  edgeR-based methods
lbs_tmm = calcNormFactors(expr_filtered, method = "TMM")
tmm     = cpm(expr_filtered, lib.size = lbs_tmm * colSums(expr_filtered))

lbs_rle = calcNormFactors(expr_filtered, method = "RLE")
rle_mat = cpm(expr_filtered, lib.size = lbs_rle * colSums(expr_filtered))

lbs_uq  = calcNormFactors(expr_filtered, method = "upperquartile")
uq      = cpm(expr_filtered, lib.size = lbs_uq  * colSums(expr_filtered))

tc      = cpm(expr_filtered)   # total count (CPM)
```

### Within lane Normalization

Concurrently, we evaluated a multi-stage normalization framework using
the EDASeq package. This track departs from the global approach of edgeR
by isolating sample-specific biophysical artifacts (within-lane bias)
and coupling them sequentially with global cross-lane adjustments
(between-lane bias).

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# --- EDASeq within-lane (GC correction) + upper-quartile between-lane ---
wt      = withinLaneNormalization(set, "gc", which = "upper", offset = TRUE)
set_uq  = betweenLaneNormalization(wt,  which = "upper", offset = TRUE)
set_full = betweenLaneNormalization(wt, which = "full",  offset = TRUE) 

full    = set_full@assayData$normalizedCounts
uq_eda  = set_uq@assayData$normalizedCounts

```

### Global Expression Distribution Diagnostics Across Six Normalization States

To visualize how different statistical corrections reshape the
distribution of reads in the dataset, we generated sequential
$\log_2(Count + 1)$ boxplots across six successive stages of data
processing. This comparative layout maps the distribution of the
transcriptomic data from its raw, unnormalized state through four
individual scaling methods: Total Count (CPM), Relative Log Expression
(RLE), Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM), and Upper Quartile (UQ). In the
end, it shows the result of the EDASeq full normalization pipeline.

By looking at these panels, we can evaluate how effectively each method
balance the distribution and stabilize sample medians, without
distorting the underlying biological variance.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, boxplot-norm1, fig.width=11, fig.height=18}

#comparative normalization diagnostic boxplots
#objective: To evaluate, compare, and select the optimal normalization method 
#by monitoring how different strategies align global gene expression across all samples.
par(mfrow = c(6, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 2, 1))

# Raw Counts:Exposes baseline technical variations.
boxplot(log2(expr_filtered + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(count+1)",
        main = "Raw counts", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# Total Count (CPM - Counts Per Million): A basic library-size scaling method. 
boxplot(log2(tc   + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(CPM+1)",
        main = "Total count (CPM)", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# RLE (Relative Log Expression Normalization): Forces the samples to align 
#based on a median gene pseudo-reference.
boxplot(log2(rle_mat + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(CPM+1)",
        main = "RLE", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# TMM (Trimmed Mean of M-values): The standard edgeR normalization. 
#It handles composition bias by trimming away highly variable and lowly expressed genes 
#before calculating scaling factors.
boxplot(log2(tmm  + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(CPM+1)",
        main = "TMM", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# Upper Quartile: Scales counts based on the 75th percentile of expression  
boxplot(log2(uq   + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(CPM+1)",
        main = "Upper quartile", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# EDASeq full (GC + Between-Lane Normalization): It explicitly corrects 
#for GC-content and gene length biases
boxplot(log2(full + 1), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
        col = col, ylab = "log2(normalizedCounts+1)",
        main = "EDASeq full (GC + between-lane)", xaxt = "n")
legend("topright", legend = names(colorMap),         
       col = colorMap, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)


par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The initial Raw Counts panel highlights substantial technical noise, showing visible discrepancies in box heights, interquartile ranges, and median alignments across the libraries due to variations in sequencing depth. In the next plot, Total Count (CPM) normalization scales the data globally to correct for library size, which narrows the variance but still leaves noticeable unevenness in the medians and spreads between different biological groups.

The advanced methods (RLE, Upper Quartile, and EDASeq full) show significant improvements over raw counts. They successfully flatten the dataset and bring the samples into a much closer global alignment. However, despite these corrections, subtle box-to-box fluctuations and minor shifts in the horizontal baseline still persist between the experimental genotypes and timepoints.

The most optimal and uniform alignment is achieved via TMM (Trimmed Mean of M-values) normalization. 
This method effectively neutralizes both sequencing depth discrepancies and sample-specific composition biases without obscuring or over-smoothing the underlying biological variation.

### Effect of normalization on library size

To evaluate how the Trimmed Mean of M-values
(TMM) workflow i,pacts on our data, the distribution statistics of the library
sizes was analyzed across all samples before and after
transformation.

Prior to normalization, the raw library sizes exhibit massive
mathematical scales, with a median sequencing depth exceeding 258
million reads per sample and a high degree of dispersion with a Coefficient of Variation (CV) of 22.45%.                   

To address these discrepancies, the TMM algorithm calculates sample-specific scaling factors based on the relative expression of a trimmed baseline of moderately expressed, non-differentially expressed genes. Rather than altering the raw sequencing counts, the algorithm adjust the
library sizes to compute effective library sizes.

The global inter-sample
variability is minimized, with the Coefficient of Variation
dropping from 22.45% down to 12.24%. By compressing this technical
noise while preserving the biological differences between the 1h
and 4h timepoints, the dataset is successfully stabilized against
compositional and depth-driven biases.

```{r}
library(knitr)


lib_sizes_before = colSums(expr_filtered)
lib_sizes_after = colSums(tmm)


stats_before <- summary(lib_sizes_before)
stats_after  <- summary(lib_sizes_after)

cv_before <- sd(lib_sizes_before) / mean(lib_sizes_before) * 100
cv_after  <- sd(lib_sizes_after) / mean(lib_sizes_after) * 100

df_stats <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Minimum Library Size", 
    "1st Quartile", 
    "Median", 
    "Mean", 
    "3rd Quartile", 
    "Maximum Library Size", 
    "Coefficient of Variation (CV)"
  ),
  `Before Normalization (Raw)` = c(
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_before[1])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_before[2])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_before[3])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_before[4])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_before[5])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_before[6])), big.mark=","),
    paste0(format(round(cv_before, 2), nsmall=2), "%")
  ),
  `After Normalization (TMM)` = c(
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_after[1])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_after[2])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_after[3])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_after[4])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_after[5])), big.mark=","),
    format(round(as.numeric(stats_after[6])), big.mark=","),

  ),
```

### GC Content Bias Profiling 

To assess how nucleotide composition impacts our
sequencing data, we evaluated the relationship between gene-wise GC
content and read counts both before and after applying a within-lane
normalization framework. 

In the not normalized state, the diagnostics reveal a non-linear bias where read counts peak for genes with average GC fractions but drop off sharply as GC content increases. This curve is a classic signature of PCR amplification issues.

The post-normalization bias plots illustrate the performance of the correction framework. By flattening these curves across the entire GC spectrum, the normalization process decouples gene's physical nucleotide structure from its measured expression level. This targeted correction ensures that the remaining expression values reflect the transcript abundance rather than sequence-dependent technical artifacts.

# Differential Expression Analysis

To identify significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across
our experimental conditions (1h vs 4h across various genetic
backgrounds) and to ensure the reproducibility of our results, 
differential expression analysis was
performed using the intersection of significantly altered genes across three prominent
Bioconductor packages: edgeR, deseq2 and NOISeq.
In this way, we minimize package-specific false positives
and isolate the Differentially Expressed Genes (DEGs)
governing the p65 translocation response.


## EdgeR

With edgeR Bioconductor package we implemented a differential expression test across the genotypes and timepoints using a generalized linear model framework. 

To evaluate changes across time and genetic conditions, we combined genotype (MED12, MED24, WT) and timepoint (1h, 4h) factors into a single group variable. This parametrization was used to build an intercept-free design matrix. Following TMM normalization and empirical Bayes dispersion estimation, we applied a negative binomial generalized linear model to handle the biological variation across replicates. Then we defined explicit contrast vectors to isolate the temporal changes occurring between the 1-hour and 4-hour timepoints for each genotype separately. 

```{r edge, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

library(edgeR)

#Model matrix design by groups 
group = factor(paste(ExperimentalInfo$genotype, 
                     ExperimentalInfo$timepoint, sep = "_")) #unified variables

design = model.matrix(~ 0 + group)

#Groups to expr_prox
ExprPro = ExprSel
ExprPro$Timepoints = as.factor(ExperimentalInfo$timepoint) #add column timepoint 

dge = DGEList(counts = assay(ExprPro), group = group) #matrix with timepoints
dge = calcNormFactors(dge, method = "TMM") #add factors of normalization
dge = estimateDisp(dge, design) #how much genes varies between samples of the same group
FitEdger = glmFit(dge, design)

#names for defining the contrasts
con <- makeContrasts(
  MED12_4vs1 = groupMED12_4h - groupMED12_1h,
  MED24_4vs1 = groupMED24_4h - groupMED24_1h,
  WT_4vs1    = groupwt_4h    - groupwt_1h,
  levels = design
)

fit <- glmQLFit(dge, design) 

lrt_M12 <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = con[, "MED12_4vs1"])
lrt_M24 <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = con[, "MED24_4vs1"])
lrt_WT  <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = con[, "WT_4vs1"])

#resulting tables
MED12edger <- as.data.frame(topTags(lrt_M12, n = Inf)$table)
MED24edger <- as.data.frame(topTags(lrt_M24, n = Inf)$table)
WTedger    <- as.data.frame(topTags(lrt_WT, n = Inf)$table)


par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

#Wild Type
plotMD(lrt_WT, hl.col = c("red", "blue"), main = "WT: 4h vs 1h", cex = 0.5)
abline(h = 0, col = "black", lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)

#MED12
plotMD(lrt_M12, hl.col = c("red", "blue"), main = "MED12: 4h vs 1h", cex = 0.5)
abline(h = 0, col = "black", lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)

#MED24
plotMD(lrt_M24, hl.col = c("red", "blue"), main = "MED24: 4h vs 1h", cex = 0.5)
abline(h = 0, col = "black", lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

To visualize the distribution and magnitude of transcriptional changes
occurring during the temporal transition (4h vs. 1h) under cytokine
stimulation, we generated edgeR Mean-Difference (MD) plots across the
three genetic backgrounds.

In the plots, the X-axis represents the baseline expression level
($Average \log \text{ CPM}$), while the Y-axis displays the biological
effect size ($\log \text{-fold-change}$). Statistically significant
differentially expressed genes ($\text{FDR} < 0.05$) are highlighted in
red (up-regulated at 4h relative to 1h) and blue (down-regulated at 4h
relative to 1h), while non-significant features remain black.

The wild type plot show that under normal conditions, transitioning from 1 hour to 4 hours causes little transcriptomic upheaval. We can visualize only a small portion of upregulated and downregulated genes, which indicates a stable minimal response over time.

In contrast, MED12 and MED24 plots show a massive increase in significant altered genes. These results show that deleting or mutating MED12 or MED24 breaks the cell's normal homostatic control between 1h and 4h, triggering a cascade of differential expressed genes. 
Furthermore, in these plots the upregulated genes show a larger cloud than the downregulated genes, which indicates that the temporal response in these mutants is dominated by transcriptional activation or a failure to repress genes at 4-hour mark.

## Consensus DEGs

To ensure an unbiased comparison, we standardized the results from differential expressed algorithms: edgeR, DESeq2 and NOISeq. Since each software package utilizes its own nomenclature, statistical metrics and row-naming convention, we developed a preprocessing function (ClassificationDEA) to standardize the outputs across all genotypes. 

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#orders = EdgeR, Deseq, Noiseq

M12DEA = list(MED12edger, DeseqShrunkM12, NoiseqM12)
M24DEA = list(MED24edger, DeseqShrunkM24, NoiseqM24)
WtDEA = list(WTedger, DeseqShrunkWt, NoiseqWt)


ClassificationDEA <- function(x){
  
  #identifier cleansing
  rownames(x) <- substr(rownames(x), 1, 15)
  x <- x[!duplicated(rownames(x)), ]
  
  #statistical metric harmonization
  # FDR
  if("padj" %in% colnames(x)) x$p <- x$padj
  if("PValue" %in% colnames(x)) x$p <- x$PValue
  if("prob" %in% colnames(x)) x$p = 1 - x$prob 
  
  # logFC
  if("log2FoldChange" %in% colnames(x)) x$logFC <- x$log2FoldChange
  if("log2FC" %in% colnames(x)) x$logFC <- x$log2FC
  
  # Classification
  x$sign <- "NS"
  x$sign[x$p < 0.05 & x$logFC > 0] <- "Up"
  x$sign[x$p < 0.05 & x$logFC < 0] <- "Down"
  
  # Binary Differential Expression 
  x$DE <- 0
  x$DE[x$p < 0.05] <- 1
  
  # Odering by log 
  x <- x[order(x$logFC, decreasing = TRUE), ]
  
  return(x)
}


AnnotatedWtDEA = lapply(WtDEA, ClassificationDEA )
AnnotatedM12DEA = lapply(M12DEA, ClassificationDEA )
AnnotatedM24DEA = lapply(M24DEA, ClassificationDEA )
```

## Evaluation of Consensus Genes 

To extract a list of high reliable differential expressed genes (DEG), we implemented a custom function (ConsensusDEA) which integrates the preprocessed outputs from edgeR, DESeq2 and NOISeq to identify robust genes that are independently validated across all three statistical frameworks. 

Firstly, the function extracts the genes identified as DEG by each individual package and then it applies an intersection across the groups, extracting a list of 'robust genes'.
To measure the degree of overlap between pairs of algorithms, the function calculates a pairwise Jaccard similarity coefficient matrix, which is computed as the size of the intersection of two genes list divided by the size of their union.  

To verify that the tools agree not just on significance, but on the magnitude of change, the function builds an independent pairwise Pearson correlation matrix, which isolates the genes shared between any two methods, extracts their respective effect sizes ($logFC$), and evaluates their correlation.  

Finally, the function scrutinizes the global consensus genes to verify their directional logic, with a matrix where a gene is retained only if its mathematical sign is perfectly consistent across all frameworks.

At the end, the final high-confidence matrix is sorted in descending order to prioritize top candidates for downstream pathway analysis.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

ConsensusDEA <- function(list_matrices) {
  
  # Name assigning 
  nombres_estandar <- c("edgeR", "DESeq2", "Noiseq")
  names(list_matrices) <- nombres_estandar[seq_along(list_matrices)]
  metodos <- names(list_matrices)
  
  # DE gene extraction 
  genes_DE <- lapply(list_matrices, function(x) {
    rownames(x)[x$DE == 1 & !is.na(x$DE)]
  })
  
  # Intersection of shared genes (global consensus)
  RobustGenes <- Reduce(intersect, genes_DE)
  
  # Matriz Jaccard
  jaccard_mat <- sapply(metodos, function(a) {
    sapply(metodos, function(b) {
      u <- length(union(genes_DE[[a]], genes_DE[[b]]))
      if (u == 0) return(0)
      length(intersect(genes_DE[[a]], genes_DE[[b]])) / u
    })
  })
  
  jaccard_mat <- matrix(jaccard_mat, nrow = length(metodos), 
                        dimnames = list(metodos, metodos))

  # Labeling genes 
  TotalSummary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list_matrices, function(x) {
    data.frame(
      Up = sum(x$sign == "Up", na.rm = TRUE),
      Down = sum(x$sign == "Down", na.rm = TRUE),
      TotalDE = sum(x$DE == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  }))
  rownames(TotalSummary) <- metodos
  
  # Initialize an empty correlation matrix with method names
  cor_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(metodos), ncol = length(metodos),
                       dimnames = list(metodos, metodos))
  
  # Calculate pairwise correlations
  for (m1 in metodos) {
    for (m2 in metodos) {
      #Find genes shared between just these two specific methods
      shared_pair_genes <- intersect(genes_DE[[m1]], genes_DE[[m2]])
      
      #Only calculate correlation if they share MORE THAN 2 genes
      if (length(shared_pair_genes) > 2) {
        logfc1 <- list_matrices[[m1]][shared_pair_genes, "logFC"]
        logfc2 <- list_matrices[[m2]][shared_pair_genes, "logFC"]
        
        #Calculate the correlation for this specific pair
        cor_matrix[m1, m2] <- cor(logfc1, logfc2, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
      } else if (m1 == m2 && length(genes_DE[[m1]]) > 1) {
        # Keep perfect self-correlation on the diagonal if the method has genes
        cor_matrix[m1, m2] <- 1.0
      }
    }
  }
  
  
  
  # Robust LogFC tracking
  robust_logFC_out <- NULL
  if (length(RobustGenes) > 0) {
    logfc_matrix <- do.call(cbind, lapply(list_matrices, function(x) x[RobustGenes, "logFC"]))
    colnames(logfc_matrix) <- metodos
    rownames(logfc_matrix) <- RobustGenes
    
    if (length(list_matrices) == 1) {
      consistent_sign <- rep(TRUE, nrow(logfc_matrix))
    } else {
      consistent_sign <- apply(logfc_matrix, 1, function(row) all(sign(row) == sign(row[1])))
    }
    
    filtered_logfc <- logfc_matrix[consistent_sign, , drop = FALSE]
    
    if (nrow(filtered_logfc) > 0) {
      mean_logfc <- rowMeans(filtered_logfc)
      robust_logFC_out <- as.matrix(sort(mean_logfc, decreasing = TRUE))
      colnames(robust_logFC_out) <- "Mean_LogFC"
    }
  }
  
  return(list(
    common_genes = RobustGenes,
    summary = TotalSummary,
    jaccard_matrix = jaccard_mat,
    correlation_logFC = cor_matrix,
    robust_logFC_matrix = robust_logFC_out
  ))
}



# Run the analysis
ResultadosWT  = ConsensusDEA(AnnotatedWtDEA)
ResultadosM12 = ConsensusDEA(AnnotatedM12DEA)
ResultadosM24 = ConsensusDEA(AnnotatedM24DEA)
```

```{r, fig.width=16, fig.height=12, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## volcano plots 
Volcano = function(df, name) {
  top = df[order(df$p), ][1:20, ]

    scale_color_manual(values = c("Down"="blue", "Up"="red", "NS"="black")) +

plots_WT  = mapply(Volcano, AnnotatedWtDEA, Libraries, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
plots_M12 = mapply(Volcano, AnnotatedM12DEA, Libraries, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
plots_M24 = mapply(Volcano, AnnotatedM24DEA, Libraries, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)

#Combine into a single flat list
all_plots = c(
  list(etiqueta_fila("WT")),    plots_WT,
  list(etiqueta_fila("MED12")), plots_M12,
  list(etiqueta_fila("MED24")), plots_M24
)

# Assemble with collected legends
# The '&' operator applies the theme to ALL subplots in the patchwork
wrap_plots(all_plots, ncol = 4, widths = c(0.15, 1, 1, 1)) + 
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

To evaluate both the statistical significance and the biological effect
size of the temporal transition (4h vs. 1h), we generated a $3 \times 3$
matrix of volcano plots mapping each genetic background against our
three differential expression pipelines.
Each individual plot maps the statistical significance of a gene on the y-axis (calculated as $-\log_{10}(p\text{-value})$) against its biological effect size on the x-axis ($\log_2\text{-fold change}$). Red and blue dots represent respectively genes that are up-regulated and down-regulated at 4h respect to 1h. Black dots represent non-significative genes.

When evaluating the performance of the three pipelines horizontally across the software columns, we can see different algorithm behaviour. 
The edgeR framework demonstrates a highly classical, balanced distribution, capturing a symmetrical plot of both up-regulated and down-regulated transcripts across a smooth significance gradient. In contrast, DESeq2 exhibits a high sensitivity to low count noise in the wild-type libraries, mapping highly variable transcripts to extreme fold-change values on the horizontal axis, yet shrinking the high-confidence candidates into a tight vertical spire in the mutant groups. Meanwhile, NOISeq operates as the most conservative framework of the three. Because it relies on empirical, non-parametric probability testing rather than standard parametric modeling, its significance scales remain considerably lower, completely ignoring minor background fluctuations to isolate only the most extreme biological signals.

Looking across the biological rows reveals an unambiguous and highly reproducible cellular phenotype. In the wild-type control group, the transition from 1 hour to 4 hours is characterized by extreme transcriptomic stability, with both edgeR and NOISeq showing that the vast majority of genes remain completely unaltered. However, the moment MED12 or MED24 are deleted, this baseline homeostatic control breaks entirely. Both mutant strains trigger an explosive, genome-wide surge in differential gene expression. Crucially, this temporal response is heavily asymmetric, dominated by a massive cloud of highly significant, up-regulated genes. This consistent rightward skew indicates that the loss of either mediator subunit results in a widespread failure to repress transcripts or an uncoupled activation of gene expression over time.

When evaluating the transcriptomic response to p65 translocation during the 1h to 4h temporal transition, a visual discrepancy was observed between the differential expression pipelines. Specifically, the wild-type (WT) condition analyzed via the DESeq pipeline exhibited an anomalous volcano plot distribution, with a high density of features clustered at extreme effect sizes ($\text{logFC} \approx \pm25$ and $\pm50$). This could be due a mathematical artifact arising from low-count or zero-count genes.


### Summary table

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(kableExtra)

unificar = function(res) {
  target_methods <- c("edgeR", "DESeq2", "Noiseq")
  
  #align the General Summary block
  summary_block <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, 
                          dimnames = list(target_methods, c("Up", "Down", "TotalDE")))
  common_sum <- intersect(rownames(res$summary), target_methods)
  summary_block[common_sum, ] <- as.matrix(res$summary[common_sum, ])
  
  #align the Jaccard block
  jaccard_block <- matrix(NA, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, 
                          dimnames = list(target_methods, target_methods))
  # If it exists, map the matching rows/columns over
  if(!is.null(res$jaccard_matrix)) {
    common_jac <- intersect(rownames(res$jaccard_matrix), target_methods)
    jaccard_block[common_jac, common_jac] <- res$jaccard_matrix[common_jac, common_jac]
  }
  
  #align the Correlation block
  cor_block <- matrix(NA, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, 
                      dimnames = list(target_methods, target_methods))
  if(!is.null(res$correlation_logFC)) {
    common_cor <- intersect(rownames(res$correlation_logFC), target_methods)
    cor_block[common_cor, common_cor] <- res$correlation_logFC[common_cor, common_cor]
  }
  
  #combine blocks together
  cbind(summary_block, jaccard_block, cor_block)
}
```

## Inter-Algorithmic Performance Assessment

The comparative analysis reveals distinct variations in the detection
sensitivity of expression analysis (DEA) frameworks between the edgeR,
DESeq2, and NOISeq libraries, and across experimental conditions.

Across all genetic backgrounds, edgeR demonstrates the highest
sensitivity, consistently yielding the largest number of Deferentially
Expressed Genes, followed by DESeq2, whichconsistently acts as a more
conservative parametric capturing a narrower subset of genes. On the
other hand NOISeq proves to be an extremely conservative algorithm,
identifying significantly fewer genes, even showing nearzero detection
in the Wild Type analysis, but with increasing yield in MED12 and MED24.

This diference in gene number detection is further displayed in the
Jaccard similarity coefficients, This disparity in sensitivity results
in a relatively low exact gene identity overlap, as evidenced by Jaccard
similarity coefficients that peak at only 0.425 between edgeR and DESeq2
in the MED24 KO gene subset, and drop to near-zero when comparing NOISeq
to any of the other two parametric methods.

However, the correlation coefficients of the LogFold Change in the list
of shared genes thorughout methodologies consistently approach
linearity, with the edgeR and DESeq2 relationship from 0.782 in WT to
0.963 in MED24 KO. Despite the different metodological approaches from
parametric algorithms and NOISeq, the correlation align almost
seamlessly between them keeping coefficients above 0.879 across all
conditions.

# Clustering

Only robust genes identified intersected by edgeR and DESeq2
were retained. NOISeq was excluded from the following pipeline due
to lack of sensitivity, which failed to output a number of informative
features big enough.

To evaluate whether the robust gene expression variability can reliably
capture the differences between experimental timepoints, we implemented
an exploratory Principal Component Analysis to visually identify
clusters among biological groups. Also a pipeline was developed to
compare unsupervised clustering algorithms (Hierarchical Clustering and
K-means) using both the normalized matrix with only the robust genes
from each biological group and its corresponding PCA dimensional space.
The performance was validated using Silhouette widths and classification
accuracy metrics (ARI) using the true biological timepoint labels as
reference.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=4}
##CLUSTERING


library(cluster)
library(factoextra)
library(mclust)


ResultadosWT = ConsensusDEA(AnnotatedWtDEA[-3]) #we are not using Noiseq for wildtype, 
ResultadosM12 = ConsensusDEA(AnnotatedM12DEA[-3])
ResultadosM24 = ConsensusDEA(AnnotatedM24DEA[-3])#reasons shown above   



# subsetting tmm matrix 
tmmWt = tmm[ResultadosWT$common_genes,ExperimentalInfo$genotype == "wt"]
tmmMED12 = tmm[ResultadosM12$common_genes, ExperimentalInfo$genotype == "MED12" ]
tmmMED24= tmm[ResultadosM24$common_genes, ExperimentalInfo$genotype == "MED24" ]


par(mfrow = c(1,3))
```

The Principal Component Analysis confirms that when stratifying the data
by genotype, the temporal expression variability between the 1 hour and
4 hour timepoints comes out. In all genotype groups the 1st PC acts as
the primary axis of separation, capturing 45% to 55% of the total
variance.

```{r, cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE,  fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
truth = as.factor(ExperimentalInfo$timepoint)
LabelsWT = as.factor(ExperimentalInfo$timepoint[ExperimentalInfo$genotype == "wt"])
LabelsMED12 = as.factor(ExperimentalInfo$timepoint[ExperimentalInfo$genotype == "MED12"])
LabelsMED24 = as.factor(ExperimentalInfo$timepoint[ExperimentalInfo$genotype == "MED24"])


ClustersPCA = function(x, k, truth){
  
  # PCA
  pcaRobustG = prcomp(t(log1p(x)), scale. = TRUE)
  
  
  #the components are either 20 or the total number if its lower than 20 
  n_pcs = min(20, ncol(pcaRobustG$x))
  pca_scores = pcaRobustG$x[,1:n_pcs, drop = FALSE]
  
  #PCA distance
  dist_pca = dist(pca_scores, method = "euclidean")
  
  #hierarchical PCA
  hc_pca = hclust(dist_pca, method = "complete")
  gr_hc_pca = cutree(hc_pca, k = k)
  
  # Kmeans PCA
  set.seed(123)
  km_pca = kmeans(pca_scores, centers = k, nstart = 25)
  gr_km_pca = km_pca$cluster
  
  # Silhouette PCA
  sil_hc_pca = silhouette(gr_hc_pca, dist_pca)
  sil_km_pca = silhouette(gr_km_pca, dist_pca)

  # no PCA
  
  mat = t(log1p(x))
  mat = t(scale(t(mat))) #scaling
  dist_raw = dist(mat, method = "euclidean")
  
  # hierarchical raw
  hc_raw = hclust(dist_raw, method = "complete")
  gr_hc_raw = cutree(hc_raw, k = k)
  
  # Kmeans raw
  set.seed(123)
  km_raw = kmeans(mat, centers = k, nstart = 25)
  gr_km_raw = km_raw$cluster
  
  # Silhouette raw
  sil_hc_raw = silhouette(gr_hc_raw, dist_raw)
  sil_km_raw = silhouette(gr_km_raw, dist_raw)
  

  
  par(mfrow = c(2,2))
  
  plot(sil_hc_pca,main = "HC PCA",col = "violetred2",border = NA)
  plot(sil_km_pca,main = "Kmeans PCA",col = "orange",border = NA)
  plot(sil_hc_raw,main = "HC Raw",col = "steelblue",border = NA)
  plot(sil_km_raw,main = "Kmeans Raw",col = "darkgreen",border = NA)
  
  
  # ARI
  
  cat("Kmeans PCA ARI:", adjustedRandIndex(truth, gr_km_pca), "\n")
  cat("HC PCA ARI:",adjustedRandIndex(truth, gr_hc_pca), "\n")
  cat("Kmeans Raw ARI:",adjustedRandIndex(truth, gr_km_raw), "\n")
  cat("HC Raw ARI:",adjustedRandIndex(truth, gr_hc_raw), "\n")
}


# Clustering functions

#Total normalized tmm 
ClustersPCA(tmm,2,truth )

# Hierarchical and Kmeans Clustering normalized Wild Type 
ClustersPCA(tmmWt,2, LabelsWT)

# Hierarchical and Kmeans Clustering normalized MED12
ClustersPCA(tmmMED12, 2, LabelsMED12)

# Hierarchical and Kmeans Clustering normalized MED24
ClustersPCA(tmmMED24,2, LabelsMED24)


```

## Clustering Validation

Analysis of the pooled dataset (n = 76) revealed that global
transcriptomic variance entirely masked temporal patterns; both
Hierarchical Clustering (HC) and K-means failed to replicate timepoint
categories (ARI approx. 0.00). However, stratifying the data by genetic
background again improved biological signals. For the Wild Type (n = 21)
and MED24 KO (n = 31) cohorts, complete-linkage HC on raw data was
highly vulnerable to high-dimensional noise, yielding severe
misclassifications (ARI = 0.357 and 0.282, respectively). However,
pre-filtering variables via Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
successfully neutralized this background noise to achieve a flawless
reconstruction of ARI = 1.000, but an average silhouette width of \>=
0.29. On the other hand, K-means demonstrated superior clustering power
by maintaining an ARI = 1.000 across both raw and PC spaces compared to
Hierarchical clustering .

Conversely, the MED12 KO cohort (n = 24) obtained a better performance
on hierarchical clustering over k-mean partitioning, both raw and PC
space HC achieved an ARI = 1.0, whereas K-means an ARI = 0.833.

These exhibits that while PCA dimensionality reduction is useful for
stabilizing hierarchical frameworks against high-dimensional noise, the
most accurate choice of clustering algorithm becomes highly variable
across biological backgrounds.

# Functional Over-Representation (ORA)

The primary objective of this section is to identify transcripts onto
biological pathways, moving the resolution from individual genes to
functional processes. Here we can obtain the change in functional
landscape across timepoints within each of the three distinct genetic
backgrounds.

We executed a three functional enrichment pipeline across the 3
genotypes to map transcriptomic differences during the 1h to 4h temporal
points. First, using consensus robust genes we conducted a comparative
over-representation analysis using KEGG, Reactome, and GO Biological
Processes. Second, we applied Gene Set Enrichment Analysis on the mean
logFC-ranked consensus gene lists from EdgeR and EDAseq and used GSEA
ridgeline plots to visualize the distribution of gene expression changes
($logFC$) for statistically significant biological pathways. Third, from
the unpooled logFC-ranked gene list (only DESeq2), we performed the
following analysis: running enrichment score for I-kappaB
kinase/NF-kappaB signaling (GO:0007249) and structural pathway mapping
via "pathview" to visualize logFC expression dynamics directly onto the
KEGG NF-kappa B signaling pathway (hsa04064).

```{r enrichment1,  cache=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(AnnotationDbi)    
library(clusterProfiler)  
library(ReactomePA)         
library(pathview)          
library(enrichplot)        
library(ggplot2)

library(grid)
library(png)

robust_M12 <- rownames(ResultadosM12$robust_logFC_matrix)
robust_M24 <- rownames(ResultadosM24$robust_logFC_matrix)
robust_WT  <- rownames(ResultadosWT$robust_logFC_matrix)

universo.entrez <- as.character(mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, keys = universo,
                                       column = "ENTREZID", keytype = "ENSEMBL"))

M12entrez <- as.character(mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, keys = robust_M12, 
                                 column = "ENTREZID", keytype = "ENSEMBL"))
M24entrez <- as.character(mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, keys = robust_M24, 
                                 column = "ENTREZID", keytype = "ENSEMBL"))
WTentrez  <- as.character(mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, keys = robust_WT,  
                                 column = "ENTREZID", keytype = "ENSEMBL"))

clean_data <- function(x, ids) {
  valid <- !is.na(ids)
  x_filt <- x[valid]
  ids_filt <- ids[valid]
  
  dups <- duplicated(ids_filt)
  x_filt <- x_filt[!dups]
  ids_filt <- ids_filt[!dups]
  
  final_vector <- as.numeric(x_filt)
  names(final_vector) <- ids_filt
  
  return(final_vector)
}

gene_list_all <- list(M12 = M12entrez, M24 = M24entrez, WT = WTentrez)

cc_kegg <- compareCluster(geneClusters = gene_list_all, fun = "enrichKEGG", 
                          organism = "hsa", universe = universo.entrez, 
                          pAdjustMethod = "BH", pvalueCutoff = 0.05, qvalueCutoff = 0.2)

cc_reactome <- compareCluster(geneClusters = gene_list_all, fun = "enrichPathway",
                              organism = "human", universe = universo.entrez, 
                              pAdjustMethod = "BH", pvalueCutoff = 0.05, qvalueCutoff = 0.2)

run_cc_go <- function(ont) { 
  compareCluster(geneClusters = gene_list_all, fun = "enrichGO",
                 OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db, ont = ont, universe = universo.entrez, 
                 pAdjustMethod = "BH", pvalueCutoff = 0.05, qvalueCutoff = 0.2, readable = TRUE) 
}
```

## Over-representation dotplots

Changes from 1 hour to 4 hour across all genotypes is orchestrated by an
activation of innate immune cascades, among them TNF and NOD-like
receptor pathways . The over-representation dotplots generated via
obtained from "ClusterProfiler" and "enrichplot", show that mutating
specific Mediator subunits alters the downregulation of proinflamatory
response. The MED24 KO displays a hyper-inflammatory profile,
characterized by a decoupling between innate detection and adaptive
immune bridging, showing an exclusively enriching for MyD88-independent
TLR4 signaling profile, while not displaying nor MHC Class I antigen
presentation or Interferon alpha/beta pathways.

## GSEA ridgeline and Pathview 

The GSEA ridgeline plots show that these immune clusters are actively
upregulated over time, driven by an activation of responses to bacterial
"like" molecules. Meanwhile MED12 shows leukocyte adhesion and maintain
a stable baseline for housekeeping processes like rRNA processing. MED24
shifts toward granulocyte migration and active suppression of protective
networks, among them: the integrated stress response. This highlights
that MED12 volatility is tightly restricted to acute immune cascades,
while MED24 is essential for sustaining cellular survival pathways under
inflammatory stress.

#### Evaluation of the NF-kB pathway

The running enrichment scores show a significant enrichment wave across
all three genotypes, peaking at the top of upregulated genes. To map
these changes, Pathview was leveraged to project these differential
expression values on the KEGG NF-kB signaling pathway diagram, rendering
upregulated nodes in red and downregulated nodes in green. In the
running enrichment score the MED24 KO mutant reaches a remarkably high
and compressed enrichment score peak just bellow 0.8, with deregulated
pathway nodes including TRAF, cIAP, and the IKK complex, which light up
heavily in red.

# Implementation and comparison of different Bioconductor packages

We aimed to employ alternative Differential Expression Analysis packages
to evaluate their respective results and identify a cross-validated set
of genes among them.

We achieved this by implementing both parametric and non-parametric
approaches. We used edgeR as a benchmark reference, alongside frameworks
like DESeq2 and NOISeq. While both edgeR and DESeq2 are parametric tools
that rely on a theoretical Negative Binomial curve we also implemented a
shrinkage with DESeq2 to obtain further refined results from this
package. We also implemented NOISeq (specifically the NOISeqBIO
framework) to obtain a non-parametric reference.

### EdgeR

1.  Initial data normalization via TMM Before statistical modeling,
    edgeR normalizes the raw count matrix using the Trimmed Mean of
    M-values (TMM) method. This
    algorithm calculates sample-specific scaling factors by computing a
    weighted mean of log-expression ratios after stripping away the most
    extremely expressed genes and those with extreme log-fold changes.
    By ensuring that a few highly abundant master transcripts do not
    mathematically distort the relative sequencing depth available for
    the rest of the genome, TMM establishes a highly balanced starting
    point scale across all libraries.

2.  Modeling Biological Variance via the Negative Binomial Distribution
    Because RNA-Seq datasets consist of discrete, non-negative integer
    read counts, continuous normal distributions are statistically
    inappropriate. While simple technical sequencing replication
    variance follows a Poisson distribution, true biological replicates
    introduce an additional layer of variation known as overdispersion
    in which the variance exceeds the mean expression levels, this makes
    the Negative Binomial (NB) distribution the right distribution to
    picture the biological variability.

3.  Empirical Bayes Dispersion Moderation: The Squeeze Mechanism
    Estimating an independent dispersion value for over 15,000
    individual genes using only the sample sizes is prone to error.
    EdgeR overcomes this limitation, by executing an Empirical Bayes
    (EB) moderation step, conceptually referred to as the "Squeeze" of
    dispersion across the entire transcriptome.

The mechanism follows a three-step algorithmic sequence:

The software calculates simultaneously a starting trend across all
15,000 genes named Global Trend Estimation. This captures that low-count
genes naturally display higher relative variance. After it evaluates the
raw, individual variance profile specifically exhibited by each
individual gene across its respective replicates this process ending up
with a Gene-wise Dispersion Estimation. Finally, edgeR applies a
weighted conditional likelihood approach to mathematically transform and
compress (squeeze) the unstable individual Gene-wise dispersions toward
the global trend.This mechanism balances the dataset. Outlier genes
exhibiting extreme, chaotic variance due to technical noise are scaled
down to match the consensus trend. However, genes showing unusual low
variance are scaled up. The end product in edgeR stabilizes variance
estimations and establishes a foundation for the final Generalized
Linear Model (GLM) Likelihood Ratio Tests (glmLRT).

### DESeq2

DESeq2 utilizes an alternative normalization algorithm and a specialized
shrinkage pipeline focused on effect-size calibration.

1.  Initial Data Normalization via Median-of-Ratios DESeq2 normalizes
    raw count data using the Median-of-Ratios method, this framework
    computes scaling facators which are sample-specific (size factors),
    this is achieved by first calculating the geometric mean of each
    gene across all samples, which is used as a reference sample. Then
    the ratio of each sample's counts to this reference is obtained and
    extracts the median of these ratios. Because it relies on the
    median, this normalization is very robust against individual
    outliers and composition biases.

2.  Modeling Biological Variance via the Negative Binomial Distribution
    Mirroring the edgeR framework, DESeq2 also fits the the discrete
    read counts to a Negative Binomial (NB) distribution

3.  Log-Fold Change Moderation: The Shrinkage Mechanism The challenge of
    obtaining stable log-fold change for thousands of genes,
    particularly those with low read counts, is overcomed by executing
    an Empirical Bayes moderation step focused on the "Shrinkage" of
    Log-Fold Changes (utilizing the adaptive shrinkage method (ashr),
    which is an algorithm that looks at the unique standard error of
    each individual gene and tailors the shrinkage dynamically).

The mechanism follows:

Deseq2 as EdgeR also calculates a global baseline trend for 15,000 genes
simultaneously. This outputs the distribution models the expected
distribution of log-fold changes under the conservative assumption that
the majority of genes do not change significantly.The Deseq2 library
evaluates the log-fold change and standard error exhibited by each
individual gene across its respective replicates and then a Shrinkage
Transformation can then be optionally applied. This shrinkage mechanism
balances the dataset based on the information available for each gene
Low-expression or highly variable genes that show artificially extreme,
chaotic fold changes due to random technical noise are shrunk. On the
other hand, highly expressed genes with replicate stability are left
almost unchanged, this drastically reduces false-positive rates and
corrects for effect sizes, providing a reliable starting point for
downstream pathway enrichment analysis.

### NOiseq

NOISeq is a RNA-seq differential expression analysis non-parametric
method that empirically models the noise distribution directly from the
data.

The empirical pipeline is executed through three core phases:

1.  Initial Data Normalization via TMM The raw counts are explicitly
    normalized using the Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) method within
    the noiseqbio function. This step ensures that baseline sequencing
    depth variations and compositional library biases are corrected,
    making the following empirical calculations directly comparable.

2.  Empirical Noise Distribution Modeling The core philosophy of NOISeq
    defines background noise without relying on parametric
    distributions. For every gene, the algorithm tracks two primary
    metrics between conditions: M : The Log-Fold Change D: The Absolute
    Difference. The absolute change which is the raw number of reads
    gained or lost.

Noiseqbio recognices random variation by computing baseline M and D
profiles and making all possible pairwise comparisons between biological
replicates within the exact same experimental group. Because no true
exogenous biological stimulus changes between replicates of the same
group are expected, these variations are considered noise. By pooling
these values across all features, the software constructs an empirical
"noise distribution" unique to our dataset.

3.  Probability-Based Hypothesis NOISeq compares the true M and D values
    obtained between our target conditions against the previously
    constructed empirical noise distribution. The software outputs a
    Posterior Probability of Differential Expression (q). This statistic
    measures the probability that a gene’s expression change is driven
    by true experimental conditions rather than chance. A gene is
    flagged as a high-confidence if its M and D metrics are out of the
    boundaries of the noise matrix (utilizing a strict threshold of q
    \>= 0.95).

# Biological interpretation

The NF-κB signaling pathway is a pillar of the cellular response to
inflammatory stimuli, requiring a very rigorous control to prevent
deleterious inflammation while also allowing its essential protective
acute response. Among the components of this pathway, Feldman et al.
(2019), have identified the Mediator complex, specifically the MED12 and
MED24 subunits, as major negative regulators. These findings introduce
an alternative model where the Mediator complex functions as a
"transcriptional brake," regulating the duration and magnitude of
pro-inflammatory gene expression. By comparing transcriptomic profiles
of the M12, M24, and WT clusters, our results capture the
transcriptional transition driven by Mediator subunit deficiency in
inflammatory induced conditios. The proinflammatory landscape proposed
by Feldman was coherent with our Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)
results, including the presence of the canonical NF-κB signaling
pathway, leukocyte cell adhesion, and the regulation of inflammatory
responses. Additionally, our results also provide information on the
different transcription profiles between the MED12 KO, which exhibits
stronger p-adjusted values and larger GeneRatios across specific
inflammatory pathways like cellular response to lipopolysaccharide,
while the GSEA ridge plots show that MED24 features a broader
distribution of upregulated immune-related terms (humoral immune
response, defense response to bacterium). This further aligns with
Feldman’s observation of the diferent contributions of both subunits.
Our results also suggest that Mediator complex loss also enriches for
TLR cascades, TNF receptor superfamily signaling, and cytokine-cytokine
receptor interactions, and also for pro-apoptotic signatures, suggesting
that the loss of these subunits may onset cells to programmed cell
death. The GSEA Enrichment Plots for the NF-kappa B signaling pathway
(KEGG: hsa04064)illustrate the transition from controlled physiological
activation in Wild Type to hyper-induction. WT showed robust baseline
activation curve peaking at arround 0.50, meanwhile MED12 and MED24
deficiency enrichment scores are peak around 0.70 and 0.75 respectively,
both with a distinct leftward leading-edge shift. This is further
evidenced in the Ranked List Metric y-axis, which surges from a maximum
of approximately 1.5 in WT to more than 20.0 in both knockout cell
lines. The convergence of these results show consistency with the model
in which, when MED12 or MED24 are removed, this negative regulation is
shattered, permitting the amplified and sustained expression of
mediators that orchestrate chronic inflammation.
